Alberta Report v. Alberta (Human Rights and Citizenship Comm.)

0201-09096

2002-12-10

2002 ABQB 1081

Alberta Queen's Bench

CHRR Doc. 03-032

Alberta Report,
Link Byfield and Michael Byfield

Applicants

v.

Alberta Human Rights and Citizenship Commission,
Harvey Kane and
The Jewish Defence League of Canada

Respondents

Date of Decision:

December 10, 2002

Before:

Alberta Queen's Bench, Clark J.

Appeal from:

(sub nom. Kane v. Alberta Report)

(2002),
2002 CanLII 78263 (AB HRC)
,
43 C.H.R.R. D/112 (Alta. H.R.P.)

Action No.:

0201-09096

Appearances by:

Dan Scott, Counsel for the Applicants

Janice R. Ashcroft, Counsel for the Respondent Commission

Greg Rodin, Counsel for the Respondent Harvey Kane and The Jewish Defence League of Canada

EVIDENCE — expert evidence — sufficient evidence and case to meet — judicial notice — NATURAL JUSTICE — right to a fair hearing — right to rebut evidence and cross-examine witnesses

Summary:
Alberta Report, an Alberta-based magazine, appealed a ruling of the Alberta Human Rights Panel that found that it had violated s. 2(1)(a) of the Human Rights, Citizenship and Multiculturalism Act ("HRCMA") by publishing an article that discriminated against Jewish persons.

Alberta Report appealed this ruling on the grounds that the Panel relied on evidence introduced before other tribunals, and violated the respondent's right to know the case to be met.

The Court of Queen's Bench found that the Panel did rely on expert evidence set out in Canadian Jewish Congress v. North Shore Free Press Ltd. and Collins v. Abrams (No. 3), decisions which were submitted to the Panel by the intervener, the Women's Legal Education and Action Fund. The expert evidence from these cases indicates that anti-Semitism is still prevalent in Canadian society and that anti-Semitism is characterized by the notions that there is a conspiracy among Jews, that Jewish people are greedy and focussed on money, and that Jewish people are deceptive and disloyal. The Court found that this expert evidence provided the context against which facts were assessed to determine that Alberta Report contravened the HRCMA.

The Court of Queen's Bench asked the question: did the Panel breach the rules of natural justice by relying on expert evidence from another case?

The Court found that the Panel is permitted to take judicial notice of certain facts and circumstances. To require complainants and human rights commissions to call expert evidence in every case to prove that a certain group experiences discrimination, or certain forms of discrimination, would defeat the purpose of the legislation because it would make adjudication unwieldy.

Nonetheless, the Court found that when the Panel intends to take notice of evidence that was originally presented before another adjudicative body, it must inform the parties of the evidence on which it intends to rely and allow the parties to challenge that decision and submit other evidence.

The Court concluded that the Panel erred by failing to give notice to the parties, and remitted the matter back to the Panel for a new hearing.

(2001),

INTRODUCTION

[
1
]  This is an appeal from the April 30, 2002, decision of the Alberta Human Rights Panel [reported
(sub nom, Kane v. Alberta Report),

2002 CanLII 78263 (AB HRC)
,
43 C.H.R.R. D/112
] (the "Panel") made pursuant to s. 33 of the
Human Rights, Citizenship and Multiculturalism Act,

R.S.A. 1980, c. H-11
.7. At issue is the extent to which the Panel can take notice of evidence introduced before other tribunals, and whether, in this instance, the Panel violated the Appellants' right to know the case to be met. I would allow the appeal and remit the matter back to the Panel for rehearing.

FACTS

[
2
]  In the October 13, 1997, edition of its magazine, the Alberta Report published an article about a failed real estate deal involving a local developer, Mr. Schickedanz, and an American promoter. At the end of the article, an uncredited source is quoted as saying:

North American commercial real estate is dominated by firms that often happen to be Jewish owned (e.g. Oshawa and Canmore Development). The retail sector is much the same. Like cliques everywhere, some of these people tend to deal with each other, and Mr. Schickedanz is an outsider.

[
3
]  Harvey Kane and the Jewish Defence League of Canada (of which Mr. Kane is the executive director) filed a complaint with the Alberta Human Rights and Citizenship Commission (the "H.R.C.C."), naming the Alberta Report, Link Byfield, Michael Byfield, and Ted Byfield. Mr. Kane alleged that the article promoted discrimination and possibly promoted hatred against Jewish people. The use of the apparently unrelated and uncredited comment at the end of the article was specifically noted but it was also alleged that the tone of the article as a whole was anti-Semitic.

[
4
]  Mr. Kane's complaint was initially dismissed by the Director but, upon reinstatement by the Chief Commissioner, Mr. Kane was charged with carriage of the matter. It was his responsibility to put the case against the Alberta Report before the Panel. In doing so, Mr. Kane called only himself as a witness.

[
5
]  Link Byfield represented the respondents and was the only person to testify on their behalf. He submitted that the article did not contravene the
Human Rights, Citizenship and Multiculturalism Act.

[
6
]  The Women's Legal Education and Action Fund ("L.E.A.F.") acted as an intervener in relation to some of the legal issues that were raised.

[
7
]  The Panel found that the Alberta Report, Michael Byfield, and Link Byfield had violated s. 2(1)(a) of the
Act:

2(1)    No person shall publish, issue or display or cause to be published, issued or displayed before the public any statement, publication, notice, sign, symbol, emblem or other representation that

(a)   indicates discrimination or an intention to discriminate against a person or a class of persons . . .

because of the race, religious beliefs, colour, gender, physical disability, mental disability, age, ancestry, place of origin, marital status, source of income or family status of that person or class of persons.

[
8
]  The Panel dismissed the complaint under s. 2(1)(b), which involves the exposure of "a person or a class of persons to hatred or contempt".

[
9
]  In making its decision, the Panel referred to two letters that formed part of the original complaint but were arguably not admitted as evidence. It also relied on expert evidence given before another tribunal and quoted in cases provided to the Panel by L.E.A.F.:
Canadian Jewish Congress v. North Shore Free Press Ltd. (No. 7)

(1997),
1997 BCHRT 35 (CanLII)
,
30 C.H.R.R. D/5 (B.C.H.R.T.)
; and
Abrams v. North Shore Free Press Ltd. (No. 3)

(1999),
1999 CanLII 35208 (BC HRT)
,
33 C.H.R.R. D/435 (B.C.H.R.T.)
. The Panel introduced this evidence by saying "Although no expert evidence was called in this case, it is helpful to consider the evidence, which is the basis for previous tribunal and court decisions" (p. 14 [D/117, § 45]).

[
10
]  From
Canadian Jewish Congress,
the Panel relied on the evidence of Professor Morton Weinfield to show that anti-Semitism is still prevalent in Canadian society but is now more subtle. He described three elements of modern anti-Semitic thought: (1) the notion of conspiracy; (2) the idea that Jewish people are "particularly greedy and focussed on money"; and (3) the belief that Jewish people are dishonest, deceptive, and disloyal (p. 14 [D/117],
citing
Canadian Jewish Congress
at § 91).

[
11
]  From
Abrams,
the Panel imported into its decision the testimony of two expert witnesses. The Panel summarized Dr. Henry's opinion that modern anti-Semitism takes the form of Holocaust-denial and conspiracy theories, including control of government. The Panel also noted the expert's opinion that racism can be hidden in popular culture, in the words and descriptions of the media (p. 15 [D/117], referencing
Abrams
at § 52).

[
12
]  The Panel also utilized the opinion of Dr. Hill, who offered examples of anti-Semitism, including the myth of a Jewish plot or conspiracy and the idea that Jewish people dominate many aspects of modern life and institutions (p. 15 [D/117], referencing
Abrams
at § 62–63).

[
13
]  While this material was quoted during the Panel's discussion of s. 2(1)(b), the expert evidence was used implicitly by the Panel to find that "the stereotype of Jews contained in the Article indicates discrimination because it discloses a discriminatory belief or attitude that will reinforce prejudice against them" (p. 19 [D/118, § 63]). The expert evidence provided the context against which the facts of the case were assessed to determine that the Alberta Report, Link Byfield, and Michael Byfield had contravened s. 2(1)(a) of the
Act.

ISSUES

[
14
]  At issue in this appeal is whether the Panel applied the principles of natural justice and allowed the Alberta Report to know the case to be met (the
audi alteram partem
rule). Three specific issues are raised in the appellants' argument:

1.    Did the Panel breach the rules of natural justice by relying on undisclosed expert evidence?

2.    Did the Panel breach the rules of natural justice by considering letters not admitted into evidence?

3.    Did the evidence support a finding that the Article was discriminatory towards Jewish people?

KNOWING THE CASE TO BE MET: RELIANCE ON EXPERT EVIDENCE

[
15
]  One of the fundamental principles of natural justice is that the parties know the case to be met:
Kane v. University of British Columbia
,

1980 CanLII 10 (SCC)
,
[1980] 1 S.C.R. 1105
. The theory behind this is explained in D.P. Jones & A.S. de Villars,
Principles of Administrative Law,
3d ed. (Scarborough: Carswell, 1999) at p. 260:

The courts have consistently held that a fair hearing can only be had if the persons affected by the tribunal's decision know the case to be made against them. Only in this circumstance can they correct evidence prejudicial to their case and bring evidence to prove their position. Without knowing what might be said against them, people cannot properly present their case.

[
16
]  The Alberta Report submits that this right was breached by the Panel when it imported expert evidence from other tribunal decisions without informing the parties.

[
17
]  The H.R.C.C., supported by Mr. Kane, replies that this evidence was before all of the parties. The expert evidence was excerpted from case law submitted to the Panel by L.E.A.F. In any event, the H.R.C.C. submits that discrimination against Jewish people is something of which the Panel could take notice. To hold otherwise places too onerous a burden on parties appearing before the Panel and, often, on the H.R.C.C. itself. In every case, either the complainant or the H.R.C.C. would have to prove by expert evidence that certain groups experience discrimination in certain ways, even though this may have been proven on numerous previous occasions.

[
18
]  The Alberta Report responds by saying that, even if the Panel could take notice of this evidence, respondents appearing before the Panel must be given the opportunity to address it. Although the case law was before the Panel and was provided to all parties, this does not constitute sufficient notice.

The Law

[
19
]  In order to address this issue, it is important to focus on judicial notice, and on how this concept is applied to tribunals.

[
20
]  Traditionally, judges have been able to take judicial notice of two things: (1) notorious facts; and (2) facts capable of immediate and accurate demonstration by resort to sources of indisputable accuracy: J. Sopinka, S.N. Lederman & A.W. Bryant,
The Law of Evidence in Canada,
2d ed. (Toronto: Butterworths, 1999) at 1055;
Cherkewich v. Cherkewich

(2001),
2001 ABQB 419 (CanLII)
,
292 A.R. 281
at § 17 (Q.B.).

[
21
]  In 1998,
the Supreme Court of Canada in
R. v. Williams
, [1998] 1 S.C.R. 1128 (a case involving jury selection), permitted judges to take judicial notice of facts found on evidence in previous cases (§ 54):

Widespread racial prejudice, as a characteristic of the community, may therefore sometimes be the subject of judicial notice. Moreover, once a finding of fact of widespread racial prejudice in the community is made on evidence, as here, judges in subsequent cases may be able to take judicial notice of the fact. "The fact that a certain fact or matter has been noted by a judge of the same court in a previous matter has precedential value and it is, therefore, useful for counsel and the court to examine the case law when attempting to determine whether any particular fact can be noted": see Sopinka, Lederman and Bryant,
supra,
at p. 977.

[
22
]
In
Cherkewich
,
Veit J.
noted that
Williams
expands the bases on which judges can take judicial notice.
Williams
provides
for a third option:

Judicial notice has been described by Watt J. in
Serplus:

[para 33] Judicial notice is the acceptance of a fact or facts without formal proof. In effect, it is a substitute for proof. The principle applies to facts that are so notorious that they are not the subject of dispute among reasonable persons. This aspect of judicial notice might be described as the "everybody knows" rule. Judicial notice may also be taken of facts that are capable of immediate and accurate demonstration by resort to readily-accessible sources of indisputable accuracy. This might be termed the "anybody can find out" rule.

[para 34] It has been held that, once a judge has made a finding of fact on the basis of evidence introduced in a case, another judge in a later case in the same jurisdiction may take judicial notice of the same fact. There is, in other words, some precedential value in prior findings of fact in the application of judicial notice.
See,
R. v. Williams
, supra,

1998 CanLII 782 (SCC)
,
124 C.C.C. (3d) 481
, at p. 502
C.C.C. (3d), per McLachlin J.

This latter form of judicial notice has been described by Lord Halsbury as the right of the court to rely on "its own historical knowledge and researches": Montana Band. (paras. 17 and 18)

[
23
]  In another case, Veit J. took judicial notice of a prior finding (made after hearing evidence) about the seriousness of a specific drug. This finding had been made during a previous sentencing of the same accused:
R. v. Whittaker

(2001),
2001 ABQB 873 (CanLII)
,
301 A.R. 136
at § 26 (Q.B.).

[
24
]  Although it would appear that the scope for taking judicial notice has broadened, it is still necessary that a court inform counsel when it intends to take judicial notice of a fact. As the Alberta Court of Appeal
noted in
Levesque v. Levesque

(1994),
1994 CanLII 4486 (AB CA)
,
155 A.R. 26
(§ 39):

. . . if judges are considering taking judicial notice of a specific fact, they should advise counsel. This may be done informally in the course of a hearing. If sought, the judge should give counsel an opportunity to call evidence and to make submissions as to the appropriateness of judicial notice in the circumstances.

[
25
]  On principle, it should be easier for administrative tribunals to take notice of certain facts or circumstances. The rules of evidence do not strictly apply. As an indication of this, s. 26(2) of the
Human Rights, Citizenship and Multiculturalism Act
states:

26(2)   Evidence may be given before a human rights panel in any manner that the panel considers appropriate, and the panel is not bound by the rules of law respecting evidence in judicial proceedings.

[
26
]  Jones and DeVillars, in
Principles of Administrative Law,
explain the rationale behind this type of rule (p. 278):

To restrict their ability to take judicial notice of only notoriously known or verifiable facts would defeat one of the rationales for the appointment of specialized tribunals. The courts have recognized that this difference between themselves and tribunals implies that the more restrictive rules do not apply to administrative bodies. The requirement is that the procedure be fair. This generally involves a certain degree of disclosure. The difficult issue is what knowledge must be disclosed. Clearly, where an adjudicator has sought information from identifiable sources, these sources must be disclosed so that the individual may raise evidence to answer it.

Application to the Facts

[
27
]  Here, the Panel relied on expert evidence quoted in a British Columbia human rights panel decision. This goes beyond taking notice of factual findings. The Panel looked behind another decision to the expert evidence utilized by the decision-maker.

[
28
]  I am not prepared to accept that
the decision in
Williams
permits this. However, whether or not
Williams
allows
courts
to go this far, the use of the evidence by the
Panel
was not inappropriate. Panels are not bound by the strict rules of evidence applicable in courts of law. The Alberta Human Rights Panel was established to adjudicate claims and to protect individuals from discrimination. It must be accessible to the public. To require the complainant or the Commission to call expert evidence in each case to prove how a certain group suffers discrimination would defeat the purpose of the legislation. In this situation, it was not impermissible for the Panel to use evidence submitted before a British Columbia tribunal.

[
29
]  However, the Panel erred in not informing the parties of its intention to take notice of this evidence. This is required by the duty of fairness that administrative tribunals owe to those who appear before them. While tribunals have more latitude in gathering evidence, this does not permit them to circumvent the requirement that they inform parties of the evidence on which they intend to rely.

[
30
]  In this case, the H.R.C.C. argues that sufficient notice was given since the evidence relied on was cited in cases provided to all parties. This is not sufficient notice. Case law is presumptively submitted to speak to points of law or to draw analogy. In this case, it was not submitted as evidence. However, the Panel used the case law as such. To ensure fairness, the Panel must inform the parties about any evidence that it intends to consider, which has not been formally admitted. If the Panel is planning to rely on expert evidence quoted in another decision, the Panel must inform all parties of this — this can occur during or after the hearing — and allow parties to: (1) address whether the evidence should be admitted; (2) challenge the weight to be accorded to the evidence; and (3) submit other evidence in rebuttal.

[
31
]  Because the Panel did not do this, I would allow the appeal.

CONCLUSION

[
32
]  Because of my finding on the first issue, it is unnecessary to address the Alberta Report's other grounds of appeal.

[
33
]  I allow the appeal and remit the matter back for a new hearing.
